accroche: Everyone knows the beginning. Almost no one knows the end, and the end is what matters.
contenu_vulgarise:
Men have been chained since childhood at the bottom of a cave, facing a wall. Behind them burns a fire; between the fire and them, carriers pass objects whose shadows are cast on the stone. These shadows are all they have ever seen. They take them for reality, and nothing in their experience suggests otherwise.

Plato places this account in Book VII of the *Republic*. It is usually summarized like this: we live in illusion, and philosophy gets us out of it. That is accurate. It is also half of the text.

## The Ascent

A prisoner is freed. The climb is painful: the light blinds him, and he needs time to make out first the reflections in the water, then the objects themselves, and finally the sun. Plato describes a gradual adjustment, not a revelation. The order of the stages matters: one does not go from shadows to sun in a single leap. Truth is not given all at once; it is learned the way one learns to see, and whoever claims to have skipped the stages has seen nothing at all.

## The Return, Always Glossed Over

Now comes the part that summaries drop. The prisoner goes back down.

Down below, his eyes, accustomed to the sun, can make out nothing in the dim light. He stumbles, gets the shadows wrong, appears less competent than those who never moved. They laugh at him. And Plato adds a sentence that changes the scope of the whole text: if this man set out to untie them and make them go up, would they not kill him, if they could lay hands on him?

It is hard not to read an allusion to Socrates here, sentenced to death in 399 BCE, whose student Plato had been some twenty years before writing these lines. The allegory does not only tell of the access to knowledge. It tells what the city does to the one who comes back from it.

## What This Shifts

Read in full, the cave is not an optimistic text about education. It is a text about the political cost of knowledge. The philosopher is not rewarded there: he is at a disadvantage, clumsy in the world of shadows, and suspect for that very reason.

An unpleasant question remains, and it is still open. Does the one who has ascended have a duty to go back down? Plato answers yes, and all of his politics rests on that yes. Nothing obliges us to follow him.

citation.texte: Will they not say that by going up there he has lost his sight; that it is not worth the trouble to try to leave the place where they are; and that if anyone takes it into his head to want to draw them out of it and lead them up, they must seize him and kill him, if possible.
citation.source: The Republic, Book VII, 517a - French translation by Victor Cousin (1822)

carte.punch: Everyone knows Plato's cave. Almost no one knows the end.
carte.idee: The freed prisoner goes back down. Below, blinded by the dim light, he appears more incompetent than those who never moved. And Plato asks: would they not kill him? His teacher Socrates had been sentenced to death.
carte.source_courte: Plato, The Republic VII, c. 375 BCE

quiz.question: What happens in the part of the allegory that summaries most often leave out?
choix: The object carriers eventually free themselves from the fire in turn
The prisoner goes back down, can see nothing, and is mocked, even threatened
The fire goes out and the cave becomes completely dark
The prisoners discover that the shadows are made on purpose for them
quiz.explication: The account does not stop at the exit: Plato has the one who has seen the sun go back down. Blinded by the dim light, he becomes clumsy where the others are at ease, and Plato suggests that they might kill him, a probable echo of the trial of Socrates. It is this second half that makes the cave a political text, and not a mere praise of instruction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what order does the freed prisoner come to see?
choix: First the sun, then the objects, finally the reflections in the water
First the reflections in the water, then the objects, finally the sun
First the objects, then the sun, finally the shadows on the wall
All at once, the moment his chains fall off
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Plato describes a gradual adjustment, not a revelation: the eyes move from reflections to objects, then to the sun. The order of the stages is part of the demonstration; one does not learn to see in a single leap.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does one see behind the death threat that closes the account?
choix: A probable allusion to the trial of Socrates, sentenced in 399 BCE
The memory of Plato's death, told by his own students
An Athenian law that punished those who left the city
A prophecy that Plato says he received from an oracle at Delphi
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Plato asks whether the prisoners would not kill the one who wanted to untie them. He had been the student of Socrates, sentenced to death by the city some twenty years before the writing of this passage: the connection is a probable reading, not a fact established by the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To which question does Plato answer yes, and all his politics rests on that yes?
choix: Can the prisoners free themselves without any outside help?
Are the shadows a faithful copy of the objects that cast them?
Does the one who has ascended have a duty to go back down?
Should the city forbid philosophy to the youngest?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The question of the return is the one the text leaves open for the reader, and which Plato settles for himself: yes, the one who has seen must go back down. All his politics rests on this answer, and the entry adds that nothing obliges us to follow him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is the cave not an optimistic text about education?
choix: Because Plato judges education impossible before adulthood
Because the prisoners all end up leaving together
Because the philosopher is rewarded there by the city he enlightens
Because knowledge has a cost there: the one who comes back becomes suspect
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The one who goes back down can see nothing, gets the shadows wrong and appears less competent than those who never moved. He is not rewarded, he is at a disadvantage, and suspect for that very reason: it is a text about the political cost of knowledge.
